cells.tense: Your hands are on this one, and there's no question in you about that.
cells.ask: Before you finish the next piece of this, say out loud in a sentence or two what it asked of you to make — and leave it standing there, without softening it or tacking a joke onto the end.
cells.core:
The shared thing you keep stays alive because you keep showing up for it. You're the one who hears when a ritual has gone stiff and finds the small way to loosen it. You know what to carry forward and what to let go quiet, and the people around you feel the difference even when they can't say what changed.

What it's cost you to keep this going is real and mostly unsaid, and most days that's fine. Saying one piece of it to the person it lands on closes a piece of work instead of letting it run on past its end. What that buys you isn't credit. It's a hand back.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending this by hand, and it's working.
cells.verb: tending what grows, where the people who inherit it can see it tended
cells.place: the common ground where a people keep what they've agreed is worth keeping

cells.tense: Your hands are on a version of this that hasn't shown up yet, and you're already holding it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been managing ahead of its time and hand it to whoever it actually belongs to — one item, today, with a sentence that says it's theirs to run now.
cells.core:
On an ordinary week when this is steady, you tend what's on the table in front of you and stop when it's tended. Work gets handed over. Other people carry their own share. You sleep at night. Nobody's holding tomorrow's problem in their lap.

What's actually running is the looking-after done a season or a year ahead of schedule. You're holding what next spring will need, gripping what hasn't come asking yet, and that grip is eating the thing the care was supposed to serve. People know when they're being kept and when they're being managed, even when both wear the same face.

cells.tense: You walked out of this one a while back, and your hand hasn't found the door since.
cells.ask: Take one thing you used to keep — a meal, a call, a shared habit — and do it this week with one other person, badly, without explaining why or asking whether it's still wanted.
cells.core:
On the days when this holds, somebody shows up for the plain version of it. You put the thing on the table. Someone else brings what they bring. You keep the version you actually have instead of the one that would look right in a photograph, and the ordinary version turns out to be enough.

What's running is the staying-away. The shared thing hasn't gone anywhere — it's still kept by whoever's tending it now — you're just not standing in it, and the absence has started to feel like a place you live rather than a gap. The wish hasn't stopped. The showing-up has.

cells.tense: Your hand is on this right now, and you'd tell anyone it's just how the days go.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do to keep this alive and call it yours — to one person, in a plain sentence, without tagging it as what anyone would do.
cells.core:
When a week goes well here, the people close to you know which parts are yours. You can say what you're keeping and why, and the saying turns out to be part of the keeping. Nothing hangs in the air unnamed.

What's running now is the doing without the saying. The small untracked things you do to hold this in place are real work — the call you make, the note you keep, the thing you remember to bring — and you keep calling them the situation instead of something you chose to do. That story isn't false. It's just missing the part where it's you.

attempts.check: The record says Stewardship (Bound) at Status 2 (Too Much) is drawn with a DIAGONAL medicine to Fulfillment, but the card's own 'in full' places its number at 2 (Balanced/Decisive) — the inner face of the Spirit pair. So the excess cannot be read as 'hoarding' or 'clinging', which would be Too Little; it has to be the future-pushed version of decisive-tending. The reader could object that 'two plates spinning' sounds like overwhelm rather than stewardship, so the core needs to show the pushing as the form care has taken — not the person's life being too full. The ask still works if the read is wrong: showing one piece of the work unfinished to one person is useful whether the person is over-extending or simply over-functioning. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any line that sounds wise about 'handing down' or 'holding space'; those come out.
